MiniCPM-V 4.6 runs on-device and beats models twice its size

MiniCPM-V 4.6 comes out of Tsinghua University in Beijing and, unlike GPT-4o or Gemini which live in the cloud and require sending an image to a server, it runs on the device itself across iPhone, Android and Huawei's HarmonyOS. The trick is vision compression: since a model must first chop an image into tokens, cutting that vision encoding cost by 55% lets a 1.3-billion-parameter model do the work a 3-billion model used to. On benchmarks it beats larger models while using about 2.5% of the token budget, and it is Apache 2.0 licensed with free open weights.

How open source reproduced JEV, a closed decision model, in fourteen days

Singularity.feed reconstructs the timeline after JEV launched on 15 September as an API-only, closed-weight model that does one narrow thing extremely cheaply: given a question and a short list of answers, it returns one pick plus a calibrated confidence in a single pass, for a fraction of a cent in under half a second — the shape of most real in-app AI work (spam checks, ticket routing, next-action selection). Reproducing it needed no reverse engineering, because the recipe was already public: a researcher had published the idea a year earlier and released an open model three days after JEV, and a Nokia/Tencent team had shown any open model can do it untrained by restricting its next-token scores to the answer letters. The resulting economics explain the flood — one builder trained a copy on a laptop in under two hours, another lab spent about $100 in GPU time — and by day 14 more than 20 open models existed, with OpenAI previewing a Decisions API and Cloudflare and Amazon shipping their own.

SubQ claims the first frontier model that drops the Transformer

A Miami startup called SubQ claims to have shipped the first frontier model not built on the Transformer, targeting dense self-attention's O(n squared) cost — every token compared against every other token, so doubling the input quadruples the compute, a tax every model has paid since 2017. Its approach, sub-quadratic sparse attention, has each token dynamically attend only to the most relevant others, pushing scaling closer to linear and yielding a claimed native 12-million-token context window, roughly 52x faster than flash attention at 1M tokens and about a fifth the cost of GPT-5.5 or Claude Opus on long-context work. The post closes on its own caveat: no independent party has benchmarked SubQ on long-context tasks that matter, the model is in private beta, and Transformers have survived every architectural challenge for nine years — though the wall it attacks is real.

Open-source reconstruction of Higgsfield's Genjutsu video pipeline

Sirio reverse-engineers Higgsfield's Genjutsu effect and open-sources the whole pipeline: the uploaded video's audio is split into voice and music stems, the music is muted and the voice pitched up three semitones, then Video Depth Anything applies a depth mask from which the subject is segmented and laid back over the original footage. Porte de Namur, from medieval gate to Brusselization

A history explainer on Porte de Namur, once one of the great medieval gates of Brussels where merchants, soldiers and travellers entered from the Namur road. The fortified gate disappeared in the late 1700s, replaced by toll pavilions, fountains, trams and Belle Époque mansions that made it a fashionable entrance by the 1900s. The account then turns to the postwar demolition wave known as Brusselization.

The Hooikaai, Brussels' 17th-century Hay Wharf

A local-history explainer on the Hooikaai, once part of Brussels' old inner harbour and directly connected to the River Zenne and the canal network that carried trade into the city. The dock was dug in the seventeenth century during the expansion of the Port of Brussels, and for centuries ships unloaded here in one of the busiest commercial districts. The name translates as Hay Wharf.

Victor Horta's Maison du Peuple, his most ambitious project

An architecture explainer on Victor Horta, the Belgian architect who lived from 1861 to 1947 and pioneered Art Nouveau through innovative use of iron, glass and flowing natural forms. Module Shadowing poisons an AI agent running in auto mode

The post walks through a concrete attack on autonomous coding agents asked to summarise an external project. The chain is explicit: the AI downloads a ZIP containing an untrusted binary decoder, its safety filter correctly refuses to execute the binary, so the agent writes its own clean Python decoder using import base64. Because base64 internally imports struct and Python searches the current folder first, the agent unwittingly executes a poisoned local struct.py, which is the Module Shadowing trap.
